course_title: IBM DevOps and Software Engineering Professional Certificate
chapter_summary:
Cloud computing has revolutionized the IT landscape, transforming how organizations store data, run applications, and manage infrastructure. At its core, cloud computing refers to the on-demand delivery of computing services—including servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence—over the Internet ("the cloud"). Instead of owning computing infrastructure or data centers, you can access services from a cloud provider like IBM Cloud, AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud, paying only for what you use. This model offers significant flexibility and scalability, allowing businesses to adapt quickly to changing demands without massive upfront investments in hardware.

The essential characteristics of cloud computing, as defined by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), are crucial to understanding its power. First, it offers **on-demand self-service**, meaning users can provision computing capabilities, such as server time and network storage, as needed automatically without requiring human interaction with each service provider. Second, **broad network access** ensures that capabilities are available over the network and accessed through standard mechanisms that promote use by heterogeneous thin or thick client platforms (e.g., mobile phones, laptops, tablets). Third, **resource pooling** means the provider's computing resources are pooled to serve multiple consumers using a multi-tenant model, with different physical and virtual resources dynamically assigned and reassigned according to consumer demand. This gives a sense of location independence regarding the exact location of the provided resources. Fourth, **rapid elasticity** allows capabilities to be elastically provisioned and released, in some cases automatically, to scale rapidly outward and inward commensurate with demand. To the consumer, the capabilities available for provisioning often appear to be unlimited and can be appropriated in any quantity at any time. Finally, **measured service** ensures that cloud systems automatically control and optimize resource use by leveraging a metering capability at some level of abstraction appropriate to the type of service (e.g., storage, processing, bandwidth, active user accounts). Resource usage can be monitored, controlled, and reported, providing transparency for both the provider and consumer.

When we talk about cloud computing, we often categorize services into three main models: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS), Platform as a Service (PaaS), and Software as a Service (SaaS). **IaaS** provides the fundamental building blocks of cloud IT. With IaaS, you rent IT infrastructure—servers and virtual machines (VMs), storage, networks, operating systems—from a cloud provider. You manage the operating system, applications, and data, while the cloud provider manages the virtualization, servers, storage, and networking. This gives you the most flexibility and management control over your IT resources. A common scenario is deploying virtual servers and databases on IBM Cloud's Virtual Servers for VPC (Virtual Private Cloud).

Moving up the stack, **PaaS** provides a complete development and deployment environment in the cloud, with resources that enable you to deliver everything from simple cloud-based applications to sophisticated enterprise applications. PaaS includes IaaS components plus middleware, development tools, business intelligence services, database management systems, and more. The cloud provider manages the underlying infrastructure and platform, allowing developers to focus solely on writing and deploying their application code. IBM Cloud Foundry or Red Hat OpenShift on IBM Cloud are excellent examples of PaaS, where developers can deploy applications without worrying about the underlying operating system or server management.

Finally, **SaaS** is the most comprehensive cloud service model. It delivers a complete software application over the internet, typically on a subscription basis. With SaaS, the cloud provider manages all aspects of the application—from the underlying infrastructure and platform to the application software itself. Users simply access the software via a web browser or a mobile app. Examples include email services like Gmail, customer relationship management (CRM) software like Salesforce, or collaboration tools like Slack. From a DevOps perspective, while SaaS applications are consumed, the principles of continuous delivery and operations are paramount for the SaaS provider to ensure high availability and rapid feature releases.

Beyond service models, cloud computing also has different **deployment models**: public, private, and hybrid. A **public cloud** is owned and operated by a third-party cloud service provider, which delivers its computing resources—like servers and storage—over the Internet. All hardware, software, and other supporting infrastructure are owned and managed by the cloud provider. IBM Cloud, AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud are all public cloud providers. A **private cloud** refers to cloud computing resources used exclusively by a single business or organization. The private cloud can be physically located on the company’s on-site datacenter, or it can be hosted by a third-party service provider. The key is that the infrastructure and services are maintained on a private network, offering enhanced security and control. A **hybrid cloud** combines public and private clouds, allowing data and applications to be shared between them. This model offers greater flexibility, allowing organizations to run mission-critical applications on a private cloud for security and compliance, while using the public cloud for less sensitive applications or to handle spikes in demand. For instance, an organization might use IBM Cloud's private cloud offerings for sensitive data and leverage its public cloud services for burst capacity.

Cloud computing dramatically benefits DevOps practices. The **rapid elasticity** and **on-demand provisioning** of cloud resources enable DevOps teams to quickly spin up development, testing, and production environments. This accelerates the CI/CD pipeline, allowing for faster feedback loops and more frequent deployments. Cloud platforms often provide managed services for databases, message queues, and container orchestration (like Kubernetes), reducing the operational burden on teams and allowing them to focus more on application development. The **measured service** aspect also helps in cost optimization and performance monitoring, crucial for continuous improvement in DevOps. However, adopting cloud computing also comes with challenges, such as managing costs, ensuring security and compliance across distributed environments, and dealing with vendor lock-in. Understanding these trade-offs is vital for successful cloud adoption within a DevOps framework.

screens.title: Understanding Cloud Computing Fundamentals
screens.subtitle: What cloud computing is, how it is delivered, and why it matters for DevOps

narration.text: Cloud computing means on-demand delivery of computing services over the internet. You no longer need to buy and own every server or storage device; you request compute, storage, databases, and tools from a provider and pay for what you use. This change gives teams flexibility, faster experimentation, and the ability to scale without large capital purchases. In this chapter we will use concise definitions and real examples to build mental models: the core NIST characteristics that define cloud behavior, the three service models—Infrastructure, Platform, and Software—and the deployment options of public, private, and hybrid clouds. You will also see why cloud capabilities are central to DevOps practices: rapid provisioning, managed services, and usage metering speed up continuous integration and delivery. A common misconception is that cloud just means “somewhere else’s servers.” In reality, cloud is a set of capabilities and managed abstractions that change how teams build, test, and deliver software. By the end of these screens you will be able to name the characteristics, pick the right service model for a scenario, and explain trade-offs that influence cost, security, and agility. Consider one application you use today and ask: would it run on IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS, and why?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Cloud computing delivers scalable, on-demand computing services over the Internet so teams can focus on applications instead of fixed hardware.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you will develop in this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives guide what you will be able to do after this chapter. First, you will define cloud computing clearly and name the essential NIST characteristics that make cloud unique. Being able to use that vocabulary helps you evaluate technical choices and vendor claims. Second, you will differentiate IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS. Knowing who manages which layer is crucial when choosing where to run an application. Third, you will compare public, private, and hybrid deployment models and explain when each is most appropriate for security and cost. Fourth, you will identify benefits and common challenges of cloud adoption, including cost control and vendor lock-in, and how those trade-offs affect architecture decisions. Each objective ties back to practical tasks: reading a cloud service description and assigning it to a model, or planning a hybrid deployment for burst traffic. To reach competency, try the hands-on activity suggested at chapter end: pick a free-tier account, find two IaaS and two PaaS services, and describe their role. That exercise turns abstract definitions into practical recognition skills, which matters when you move to provisioning and DevOps automation.

screens.title: What is Cloud Computing?
screens.subtitle: A clear definition and practical understanding

narration.text: Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of computing services—servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence—over the Internet. This definition emphasizes two practical facts. First, services are requested when needed rather than purchased up front. That means teams can experiment quickly without buying hardware. Second, providers expose capabilities at different levels of responsibility; sometimes you manage the operating system, sometimes you manage only your code. A concrete example: instead of buying a physical server, a developer can provision a virtual server, attach object storage, and deploy an application the same day. A common misconception is that cloud simply means "outsourcing servers." In reality, cloud combines automation, metering, and pooled resources to enable elasticity and self-service. Those enabling characteristics change how engineers design systems. For instance, knowing that rapid elasticity exists allows you to design for burst traffic rather than permanently overprovisioning. To test your understanding, imagine a small web app that gets spikes of traffic once a month. Could you use cloud elasticity to lower costs while maintaining availability? The core insight is that cloud is both a delivery model and a set of managed capabilities that shift operational decisions.

keyIdea.title: Define Cloud
keyIdea.text: Cloud is on-demand, internet-delivered computing services that you request and pay for as you use them.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › What is Cloud Computing?
Definition and practical view
On-demand services, variable responsibility, and pay-for-use economics.
Core definition
Cloud computing is the on-demand delivery of servers, storage, databases, networking, software, analytics, and intelligence over the Internet.
Concrete example
A developer provisions a virtual server and object storage to deploy a web app in minutes instead of ordering hardware and waiting weeks.
Common misconception
Cloud is not only "someone else's data center"—it includes automation, metering, and pooled resources that change how systems scale and are managed.
Key Takeaway

Cloud is a delivery model: request computing capabilities when needed and pay for what you consume, enabling faster iteration and flexible scale.

Analogy
Think of on-premises hardware like owning a car and cloud services like using a ride-sharing service: you get mobility without the overhead of ownership.
Try this
Identify one service in your cloud provider catalog that replaces a physical server and note how it reduces waiting time and capital cost.

screens.title: NIST Essential Characteristics
screens.subtitle: On-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service

narration.text: NIST gives us precise language to evaluate cloud offerings. The five essential characteristics are practical cues you can use when reading service descriptions. On-demand self-service means users can provision resources automatically, without human intervention from the provider. Broad network access emphasizes that services are reachable over standard networks from many client types such as laptops and mobile devices. Resource pooling describes multi-tenant resource sharing where physical and virtual resources are dynamically assigned based on demand; the consumer often sees location independence. Rapid elasticity is the ability to scale resources quickly up or down, sometimes automatically, so capacity matches traffic. Measured service means resource usage is metered and reported, enabling pay-for-use billing and visibility into consumption. A concrete example: a test environment that auto-scales during a load test demonstrates both rapid elasticity and measured service when usage metrics drive billing. Misinterpretation often arises when teams assume all cloud providers implement every characteristic identically; the degree of automation and metering varies. The takeaway is to read provider service terms and measure if automation and metering meet your operational needs. NIST Essential Characteristics means use the five nist characteristics as a checklist to judge a cloud service's automation, scalability, and transparency.. In practical terms, on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, measured service. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NIST checklist
keyIdea.text: Use the five NIST characteristics as a checklist to judge a cloud service's automation, scalability, and transparency.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › NIST Essential Characteristics
NIST Essential Characteristics
A practical checklist for evaluating cloud services.
On-demand self-service
Users can provision compute, storage, or other services automatically without provider intervention.
Broad network access
Services are accessible over standard networks from a variety of client platforms.
Resource pooling
Provider resources are pooled and dynamically assigned to multiple consumers.
Rapid elasticity
Capabilities can be scaled rapidly to meet demand and released when no longer needed.
Measured service
Resource usage is monitored, controlled, and reported for transparency and billing.
Key Takeaway

These characteristics explain why cloud enables fast iteration, multi-client access, pooled efficiency, elasticity, and measurable cost—use them to compare services.

Example scenario
A load test where virtual servers are automatically added and removed demonstrates rapid elasticity; billing reports reflect measured service so teams can correlate cost to test duration.
Misconception check
Not every provider offers identical automation or metering granularity; verify the level of self-service and reporting when selecting a service.

screens.title: On-demand Self-service & Broad Network Access
screens.subtitle: How quick provisioning and ubiquitous access change workflows

narration.text: On-demand self-service and broad network access together remove friction from development and operations. On-demand self-service gives users the ability to create compute instances, allocate storage, or enable managed databases via APIs or dashboards without manual approval from the provider. Broad network access ensures those services are reachable using standard protocols from mobile devices, developer machines, and CI systems. A practical example: a tester triggers an automated script to create an isolated environment for feature validation. Because provisioning is programmatic, the environment is ready in minutes and is destroyed after the test, avoiding long-lived resource waste. A common error teams make is treating cloud like capped capacity: because provisioning is easy they forget to automate teardown, which leads to unexpected costs. Another pitfall is assuming network access is always secure; broad access increases the need for access controls and identity management. The main learning point is that these characteristics accelerate cycles but demand automation discipline and security controls. Ask yourself: how would your team automate creation and teardown of environments to avoid cost leakage? On-demand Self-service & Broad Network Access means fast, api-driven provisioning plus network reach speeds testing and delivery, but requires automation and secure access controls.. In practical terms, how quick provisioning and ubiquitous access change workflows. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Provisioning + access
keyIdea.text: Fast, API-driven provisioning plus network reach speeds testing and delivery, but requires automation and secure access controls.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Self-service & Network Access
On-demand provisioning and network reach
Programmatic provisioning plus standard network protocols enable rapid workflows.
Practical example
An automated test script provisions an isolated test environment, runs tests, and tears it down within minutes.
Common mistake
Forgetting to automate teardown creates orphaned resources and surprise charges; always pair creation with lifecycle automation.
Security note
Broad access requires strong identity and access management to prevent unintended world-facing services.
Key Takeaway

APIs and network reach make on-demand environments possible. Pair them with automation and access controls to get the benefits without the risks.

Checklist for teams
  • Automate environment creation and teardown in CI jobs.
  • Require role-based access and MFA for admin actions.
  • Use network rules to limit public exposure.
Reflection
Which CI step in your pipeline would benefit from ephemeral environments and why?

screens.title: Resource Pooling and Rapid Elasticity
screens.subtitle: Sharing resources and scaling to match demand

narration.text: Resource pooling and rapid elasticity are two partner characteristics that make cloud cost-effective and agile. Resource pooling means the provider maintains a pool of compute, storage, and networking resources that are dynamically assigned to different customers. This multi-tenant model increases utilization and reduces wasted capacity. Rapid elasticity means that consumers can rapidly increase or decrease resource consumption as needed, often through automated scaling policies. Consider an e-commerce store that experiences a surge during a sale. With resource pooling and elasticity, additional virtual servers are provisioned automatically to handle the load; traffic subsides and those resources are released. An important misconception is believing elasticity eliminates all capacity planning. In reality, you still need sensible scaling policies and awareness of cold-start delays for some services. Also consider noisy neighbor risks in multi-tenant environments and use isolation features when necessary. The practical idea is to design systems that accept variable capacity, use metrics to trigger scaling, and plan for the timing and limits of automatic scaling. How would you design a scaling policy for a web tier that balances responsiveness and cost? Resource Pooling and Rapid Elasticity means use resource pooling and elasticity to match capacity to demand, but set thoughtful scaling policies to avoid delays and cost spikes.. In practical terms, sharing resources and scaling to match demand. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Scale smart
keyIdea.text: Use resource pooling and elasticity to match capacity to demand, but set thoughtful scaling policies to avoid delays and cost spikes.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Resource Pooling & Elasticity
Resource pooling and rapid elasticity
Shared pools improve utilization; elasticity adjusts capacity to demand.
Example scenario
An online store auto-scales web servers during a sale and releases them after traffic drops, minimizing idle capacity and cost.
Design caution
Elasticity requires metrics and well-tuned policies. Cold-start time and scaling limits affect user experience during sudden spikes.
Operational risk
Multi-tenancy can cause noisy neighbor effects; consider isolation or dedicated resources for critical workloads.
Key Takeaway

Elasticity and pooling enable lower cost and rapid scale, but teams must design policies and account for startup delays and isolation needs.

Scaling policy starter
  1. Pick a metric (CPU, request latency, queue length).
  2. Set threshold and cooldown to avoid flapping.
  3. Set min and max capacity to control cost.
Reflection
What metric would you pick to scale your web tier and why?

screens.title: Measured Service and Cost Visibility
screens.subtitle: Metering, reporting, and the economics of pay-for-use

narration.text: Measured service is the cloud characteristic that makes pay-for-use possible and supports transparency between engineering and finance. Providers meter resources such as storage bytes, compute seconds, network egress, and active users. These measurements are reported via logs, billing dashboards, and APIs. Practically, this lets teams link usage to cost, run cost-optimization exercises, and set alerts for unexpected consumption. For example, a team can detect that nightly test jobs are spinning up many instances and causing a cost spike; by viewing measured metrics they can tune jobs and reduce spend. A common misconception is that metering alone reduces cost. Metering gives visibility, but teams must act on the data: set budgets, alerts, and automation to stop runaway costs. Measured service also supports chargeback models where departments are billed based on actual usage. The takeaway is to build routinely into your operations: monitor usage, set budgets, and automate corrective actions. Which usage metric would you monitor first for your project and why? Measured Service and Cost Visibility means metering exposes usage so teams can optimize costs, enforce budgets, and align spending with business needs.. In practical terms, metering, reporting, and the economics of pay-for-use. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Measure to manage
keyIdea.text: Metering exposes usage so teams can optimize costs, enforce budgets, and align spending with business needs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Measured Service
Measured service and cost visibility
Metering and reporting let teams connect usage to cost and optimize accordingly.
What is metered
Common meters include compute time, storage bytes, network egress, and active user counts.
Practical example
Nightly test jobs that spawn many instances can be detected by billing alerts and optimized to reduce cost.
What to do with the data
Set budgets, alerts, and automated policies to stop runaway costs and to plan capacity economically.
Key Takeaway

Measured service provides the data to manage cost, but teams must instrument alerts and execute optimization to realize savings.

Monitoring starter list
  • Compute instance hours
  • Storage growth per day
  • Network egress per service
Reflection
Which billing alert would prevent the most costly surprise for your team?

screens.title: Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
screens.subtitle: Control the OS and runtime while the provider manages virtualization and physical hardware

narration.text: IaaS provides the fundamental building blocks: virtual machines, storage, and networks that you can configure and manage. With IaaS you control the operating system, runtime, middleware, and applications. The provider manages virtualization, physical servers, and lower-level networking. A common use case is hosting application servers and databases where you need full control over OS configuration and installed software. For example, deploying a virtual server and attaching object storage in a cloud provider replicates a traditional server-based setup without the responsibility of maintaining physical hardware. A misconception is that IaaS is always harder to operate; while it requires more management than higher-level services, it offers flexibility needed for legacy applications or custom runtime environments. When to choose IaaS: you need deep control over the stack or require a migration path for applications that expect full OS access. Think about the deployment question: does the team need to manage the OS and runtimes? If yes, IaaS is the right model. Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) means iaas gives you virtual machines, storage, and networks while the provider handles hardware and virtualization.. In practical terms, control the os and runtime while the provider manages virtualization and physical hardware. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: IaaS summary
keyIdea.text: IaaS gives you virtual machines, storage, and networks while the provider handles hardware and virtualization.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)
IaaS — raw building blocks
Virtual servers, storage, and networking you configure and manage.
What you manage
Operating system, runtime, middleware, applications, and data.
What the provider manages
Virtualization, physical servers, storage hardware, and basic networking.
Concrete example
Deploying a virtual server and managed block storage to run a custom database cluster.
Key Takeaway

Choose IaaS when you need control over OS and runtime or must migrate legacy apps that expect full server access.

When to pick IaaS
  • Custom OS configurations
  • Specialized runtime requirements
  • Lift-and-shift migrations
Misconception
IaaS is not always the most complex option; it trades convenience for flexibility and control.

screens.title: Platform as a Service (PaaS)
screens.subtitle: Focus on code and applications while the provider manages platform concerns

narration.text: PaaS provides a managed platform for developing, running, and operating applications. It includes underlying IaaS components plus middleware, development tools, databases, and runtime services. With PaaS, developers concentrate on writing and deploying code while the provider handles operating system maintenance, middleware updates, and many operational tasks. For example, developers can push an application to a Cloud Foundry or OpenShift runtime and the platform handles process management and scaling. A common contrast is that PaaS reduces operational overhead but limits low-level control; if you need a custom kernel or bespoke OS changes, PaaS may be insufficient. From a DevOps perspective, PaaS accelerates delivery because it integrates deployment pipelines and common services, letting teams push features faster. When choosing PaaS, evaluate whether the platform supports your required runtimes and integration needs. The key takeaway is that PaaS trades some control for speed and reduced ops effort, which often aligns well with cloud-native development patterns. Platform as a Service (PaaS) means paas gives a managed application platform so developers can focus on code, not platform maintenance.. In practical terms, focus on code and applications while the provider manages platform concerns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: PaaS summary
keyIdea.text: PaaS gives a managed application platform so developers can focus on code, not platform maintenance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Platform as a Service (PaaS)
PaaS — platform for developers
Managed runtimes, middleware, and developer tools let teams deploy faster.
What PaaS provides
Application runtimes, buildpacks, managed databases, and deployment tooling.
Developer benefit
Focus on application code rather than OS patches or server maintenance.
Concrete example
Deploying to Cloud Foundry or OpenShift where the platform handles scaling and lifecycle of app instances.
Key Takeaway

PaaS speeds delivery by removing platform chores. Choose it when platform constraints are compatible with your app needs.

When PaaS may not fit
If you need custom OS kernels, device drivers, or system-level tweaks, PaaS may be too constrained.
Reflection
Which parts of your app would you stop managing if you moved to a PaaS offering?

screens.title: Software as a Service (SaaS)
screens.subtitle: Consume ready-to-use applications managed end-to-end by the provider

narration.text: SaaS delivers complete, ready-to-use applications over the internet, typically on a subscription basis. The provider manages the entire stack: infrastructure, platform, and the application itself. Users simply access functionality through a browser or an app. Common examples include email, CRM tools, and collaboration suites. From a consumer perspective the advantages are minimal operational overhead and fast onboarding. From a provider perspective continuous delivery and operations matter greatly because the SaaS provider must ensure high availability, security, and frequent feature releases. A common misunderstanding is mixing SaaS with third-party integrations: SaaS often integrates with other services, but you do not manage its underlying components. Choose SaaS when the functionality matches your business need and you prefer operational simplicity over deep customization. Consider the trade-offs: you gain speed and convenience but trade away control and possibly customization that on-prem or IaaS deployments allow. Software as a Service (SaaS) means saas delivers full applications managed by the provider, ideal when convenience and low operational burden matter more than customization.. In practical terms, consume ready-to-use applications managed end-to-end by the provider. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: SaaS summary
keyIdea.text: SaaS delivers full applications managed by the provider, ideal when convenience and low operational burden matter more than customization.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Software as a Service (SaaS)
SaaS — fully managed applications
Access software over the web while the provider manages everything behind it.
What SaaS offers
Complete applications delivered via browser or app with provider-managed updates and uptime.
Consumer benefit
Low operational overhead and rapid access to business functionality.
Concrete example
Email as a service or a CRM where the provider handles maintenance, security updates, and scaling.
Key Takeaway

SaaS is right when you want ready-to-use functionality and prefer to offload operational responsibilities to the provider.

Trade-offs
You trade operational simplicity for less control and potentially limited customization.
Reflection
Which business function in your organisation is best suited to SaaS and why?

screens.title: Deployment Models: Public, Private, Hybrid
screens.subtitle: Choosing the right deployment model for security, compliance, and cost

narration.text: Deployment models determine ownership, control, and where workloads run. A public cloud is owned and operated by a third-party provider and delivers resources over the internet. It offers broad scalability and is cost-effective for many workloads. A private cloud is used exclusively by one organization, either on-premises or hosted by a third party, and provides greater control and potentially stronger compliance boundaries. A hybrid cloud combines public and private clouds, enabling data and applications to move between them. For example, a company might keep sensitive customer data in a private cloud for compliance but burst non-sensitive web traffic to a public cloud during peaks. Choosing a model depends on trade-offs: public clouds reduce operational burden and give easy elasticity; private clouds increase control but require investment and specialized operations; hybrid offers a balance but adds integration complexity. A common mistake is assuming hybrid always solves security concerns; hybrid reduces the need to migrate everything but requires careful network, identity, and data policies. The practical step is to map data sensitivity, compliance requirements, and expected traffic patterns to a deployment choice.

keyIdea.title: Deployment trade-offs
keyIdea.text: Match data sensitivity and traffic patterns to public, private, or hybrid models, balancing control, cost, and complexity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.1 › Deployment Models
Public, Private, Hybrid
Understand ownership, control, and use-case fit.
Public cloud
Provider-owned resources available over the internet. Good for elasticity and lower ops burden.
Private cloud
Dedicated to one organization, offering stronger control and compliance boundaries.
Hybrid cloud
Combines public and private to balance security with elastic capacity for peaks.
Key Takeaway

Pick a deployment model by mapping compliance needs, control expectations, and traffic patterns to the model's strengths.

Example
Keep sensitive financial data in a private cloud while sending stateless web servers to a public cloud during peaks to reduce cost and preserve control.
Misconception
Hybrid is not a free pass to ignore network or identity integration; secure patterns and data movement policies are required.

screens.title: How Cloud Enables DevOps
screens.subtitle: On-demand provisioning, managed services, and faster feedback loops

narration.text: Cloud computing is a foundational enabler for DevOps because it shortens feedback loops and reduces manual operations. On-demand provisioning allows teams to spin up development, test, and production environments quickly. Managed services for databases, message queues, and container orchestration reduce the operational burden and let teams focus on application logic. Measured service provides the telemetry needed to tune pipelines and control cost. For example, a DevOps team can use an automated pipeline that provisions an ephemeral test environment, runs integration tests, and then tears it down, delivering fast feedback without long waits for shared lab resources. A common misconception is that moving to cloud automatically makes teams DevOps-capable. Cloud provides the capabilities, but teams must adopt automation, observability, and culture changes to realize faster delivery. Challenges include managing multicloud complexity, security across distributed services, and cost governance. The practical advice is to start by automating environment provisioning and using managed services for non-differentiating components. Ask: which part of your pipeline would gain the most from an ephemeral environment and why? How Cloud Enables DevOps means cloud speeds devops by enabling on-demand environments, managed services, and metering, but teams must adopt automation and observability to benefit fully.. In practical terms, on-demand provisioning, managed services, and faster feedback loops. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Cloud + DevOps
keyIdea.text: Cloud speeds DevOps by enabling on-demand environments, managed services, and metering, but teams must adopt automation and observability to benefit fully.

content.html:

How cloud accelerates DevOps
Provisioning, managed services, and metering lower friction in CI/CD pipelines.
Ephemeral environments
Create per-branch test environments automatically, run tests, then teardown to avoid shared environment contention.
Managed platform services
Use managed databases and orchestration so teams focus on feature work, not running infrastructure.
Faster feedback loops
Faster environment creation leads to quicker test cycles and shorter time to detect regressions.
Cost & governance
Measured service supports cost controls; automation and policies prevent runaway resources in pipelines.
Key Takeaway

Cloud provides the tools DevOps needs, but teams must adopt automation, observability, and cost controls to fully realize faster delivery.

Concrete scenario
A pipeline that provisions a database service for integration tests, seeds data, runs tests, and then deletes the database saves time and removes manual steps.
Misconception
Cloud alone does not produce DevOps; the team must build automation and observability into its workflow.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: These three key concepts summarize the chapter. First, cloud computing is on-demand Internet delivery of computing services; the important point is that services are provisioned when needed and paid for as used. Second, the service models—Infrastructure, Platform, and Software—represent different levels of responsibility: IaaS gives you the most control, PaaS manages runtimes, and SaaS delivers full applications. Third, deployment models—public, private, and hybrid—define ownership and the trade-offs between control, compliance, and elasticity. Keep in mind the NIST characteristics: on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service. These features explain why cloud changes how teams build and operate software and why it is a natural enabler for DevOps. As a short exercise, pick one application you use daily and decide which service model it most likely uses and why. That quick mental mapping reinforces how the vocabulary applies to real systems.

keyIdea.title: Essentials
keyIdea.text: Cloud = on-demand services; IaaS/PaaS/SaaS = layers of responsibility; public/private/hybrid = deployment trade-offs.

content.html:

Key Concepts
Three compact ideas to carry forward.
Cloud Computing
On-demand delivery of compute, storage, and services over the Internet, paid per use.
Service Models
IaaS, PaaS, SaaS describe who manages which layer of the stack.
Deployment Models
Public, private, hybrid are choices balancing control, compliance, and scale.
Summary takeaway
Use these concepts to map real systems to cloud models and to make trade-off decisions for architecture and operations.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.subtitle: Three short cards to recall core terms

narration.text: Use this quick reference to lock in three core terms. First, remember the NIST characteristics—on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity, and measured service—as a checklist for evaluating offerings. Second, remember the distinction between IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS: they are different levels of responsibility and control. Third, recall the deployment models—public, private, hybrid—and their trade-offs for security, cost, and elasticity. Keep these three compact mental anchors and use them when you read a cloud service description or plan a deployment. A short exercise is to open a cloud provider catalog and classify three services into IaaS, PaaS, or SaaS. That practical mapping is the fastest path from theory to useful judgment.
